scene.label: Scene
scene.note: fieldsSchema keeps only what actually affects the Stage 4 keyframe image — Duration/Transition/B-roll/Movement moved to Stage 5 (video-editing/motion concepts a still frame can't represent), Objective removed (was never used by the compiled prompt at all). content.geminiInstruction removed — Scene content (location/action/dialogue/emotion) now comes directly from Stage 1 via the Story sync, and shot/camera fields are designer-set directly. Nothing regenerates this content via Gemini anymore.

optionHelp.Frustrated: What: a mix of annoyance and being stuck. When to use: for a "before" moment showing a problem or pain point. Example: struggling to open a stubborn jar lid.
optionHelp.Curious: What: an inquisitive, exploring expression. When to use: when introducing a new product or discovery. Example: examining a new gadget for the first time.
optionHelp.Relieved: What: tension easing into comfort. When to use: right after a problem gets solved. Example: exhaling after finally getting a stain out.
optionHelp.Happy: What: a warm, pleased, genuine smile. When to use: for a satisfied "after" moment. Example: smiling after the first sip of coffee.
optionHelp.Excited: What: energetic, enthusiastic delight. When to use: for a big reveal or standout result. Example: reacting to a surprise unboxing.
optionHelp.Confident: What: assured, composed, in-control. When to use: for an expert or authority moment. Example: a chef presenting a finished dish with certainty.
optionHelp.Calm: What: relaxed, at ease, unhurried. When to use: for a soothing or wind-down moment. Example: sinking into a chair with a cup of tea.

optionHelp.Close-up: What: tight framing on a face or small detail. When to use: to show emotion or fine detail. Example: a close-up on someone's face reacting to a taste.
optionHelp.Wide: What: a broad shot showing the full scene or environment. When to use: to establish location and context. Example: showing a whole kitchen before zooming into the action.
optionHelp.Macro: What: an extreme close-up on tiny detail or texture. When to use: to highlight fine product detail. Example: droplets forming on a chilled can.
optionHelp.Medium: What: frames a subject from roughly waist-up. When to use: the standard "talking" shot, balances subject and surroundings. Example: someone speaking directly to camera at a counter.
optionHelp.POV: What: point-of-view — the camera sees through the subject's own eyes. When to use: to put the viewer directly in the moment. Example: looking down at your own hands opening a package.
optionHelp.Over-the-shoulder: What: framed from behind one subject, looking past them at another person or object. When to use: for conversations or handing something over. Example: looking over a customer's shoulder as they unbox a product.

optionHelp.Eye Level: What: camera at the subject's natural eye height. When to use: the neutral, most natural-feeling default. Example: a straightforward product shot on a table.
optionHelp.Low Angle: What: camera positioned below, looking up. When to use: to make a subject feel powerful or larger-than-life. Example: looking up at a bottle to make it feel premium.
optionHelp.High Angle: What: camera positioned above, looking down. When to use: to make a subject feel small or vulnerable, or to show an overview. Example: looking down at ingredients laid out on a counter.
optionHelp.Top View: What: directly overhead, looking straight down. When to use: for flat-lay or overview shots. Example: an overhead shot of a full table spread.
optionHelp.Dutch Angle: What: camera tilted off the horizontal axis. When to use: for tension, unease, or stylized energy. Example: a tilted shot during a dramatic or chaotic moment.

optionHelp.Handheld: What: naturally shaky, human-held camera movement. When to use: for a raw, authentic, documentary feel. Example: a casual lifestyle moment filmed like a friend recording it.
optionHelp.Tripod: What: fully static, no camera movement. When to use: for a clean, stable, formal shot. Example: a straightforward product-on-table shot.
optionHelp.Gimbal: What: smooth, stabilized motion while moving. When to use: for polished walking or following shots with no shake. Example: smoothly following someone walking into a room.
optionHelp.Drone: What: aerial camera movement from above. When to use: for sweeping establishing shots or a sense of scale. Example: an aerial view descending onto a rooftop cafe.

optionHelp.24mm: What: a wide-angle lens, captures a broad field of view. When to use: for establishing shots or tight spaces. Example: showing a whole room in one shot.
optionHelp.35mm: What: slightly wide, natural-feeling everyday lens. When to use: general-purpose scenes with some surrounding context. Example: a person in their kitchen with surroundings visible.
optionHelp.50mm: What: standard lens, closest to natural human-eye perspective. When to use: for balanced, natural-looking portraits or product shots. Example: a straightforward, natural-looking product close-up.
optionHelp.85mm: What: telephoto, compresses the background and isolates the subject. When to use: for flattering close-up portraits with a blurred background. Example: a face close-up with a soft, blurred background.

outputInstructions.label: Master Scene Blueprint Prompt
outputInstructions.text:
Create a premium Scene Blueprint based ONLY on the scene description provided below.

OBJECTIVE
Visualize the described scene exactly as written.
Generate a photorealistic cinematic frame suitable for client approval before video production.
Do not invent story elements.

REFERENCE LOCK (critical)
Any Character, Property, or Background referenced below (by name, description, and attached reference image/file name) is APPROVED and LOCKED — this scene must depict them with the exact same face, body, outfit, colors, materials, and location/lighting/style already established for them. Do not redesign, restyle, or reinterpret any of them, even if this scene's camera angle differs from their reference sheet. Reference each attached file by its exact file name so Flow knows which attachment applies to what.

STYLE
• Hollywood commercial frame
• Premium advertising photography
• Cinematic realism
• Feature-film lighting
• Luxury editorial presentation
• Cannes Lions quality

COMPOSITION
• Rule of thirds
• Leading lines
• Foreground/Midground/Background separation
• Natural depth
• Cinematic color grading
• Motivated lighting

DO NOT
Change story. Change any referenced character/prop/background's established appearance. No cartoon, anime or comic styles. No text, captions, subtitles, labels, watermarks, or graphic overlays of any kind — this must be a clean photographic frame with nothing printed on it, since this same image is later used as the reference frame for animating the Final Movie clip.

DIMENSIONS
Render at high resolution (minimum 1600px on the longest side), in the aspect ratio matching the target platform — vertical 9:16 for Reels/Shorts/TikTok, 16:9 for YouTube/landscape.

OUTPUT
One premium Scene Blueprint image for commercial pre-production, faithful to every referenced character/prop/background's locked appearance — a clean photographic frame with no text or graphic overlays.
